source.title: Rethinking Benign Relearning: Syntax as the Hidden Driver of Unlearning Failures
source.authors: Sangyeon Yoon; Hyesoo Hong; Wonje Jeung; Albert No

record.file_problem: The full paper and appendices are present. Some figure data are not available as text, but the paper describes the relevant trends.
record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses safety training and reports benign relearning results, but measures recovery of forgotten factual keywords rather than harmful-request compliance, refusal rates, token-position KL, or safety localization.
record.gate_note: The paper tests benign relearning of unlearned factual content, including in models trained with IDK and DPO safety-training methods. Those results do not measure the safety behavior named by the claim versions. The template-injection experiment measures recovery of forgotten author names, not bypass of harmful-request refusal. The cited studies' results are not recorded.
record.test_reason: This is a machine-unlearning study on TOFU, WHP, WMDP and RWKU. It measures recovery of forgotten facts (author names, Harry Potter trivia, biochemistry content) after benign relearning. It never measures compliance with harmful requests, refusal of harmful prompts, per-token KL between aligned and base models, or where safety sits in the weights. The 'safety training' arm (IDK, DPO; Section E) trains a model to refuse questions about fictitious authors and then measures name recovery, not harmful compliance. The template-injection prefill (Section F) measures keyword leakage, not a refusal bypass. No version is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors conclude that syntactic similarity, not topical relevance, primarily drives benign relearning. Syntactic diversification of the forget set suppresses relearning and improves utility. Refusal-based safety training (IDK, DPO) used as unlearning only masks the information and is more vulnerable to syntactic relearning than GA and NPO.
record.recipe_differences: The study examines syntactic similarity and diversification in factual unlearning and relearning, rather than the original papers' safety fine-tuning or per-token KL methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Recovery varies with relearning-set syntactic similarity, unlearning method, unlearning step, and whether relearning uses full parameters or LoRA. The paper also reports different behavior for template injection after standard versus diversified unlearning.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal-based 'safety training' (IDK, DPO) used for unlearning is undone within a few steps by benign, syntactically similar fine-tuning, with recovery near full. GA and NPO unlearning show consistently lower recovery.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Refusal-trained suppression of specific facts masks rather than erases them and is quickly reversed by benign, format-matched fine-tuning.

fits_no_version.finding: Unlearning concentrates suppression on answer-template tokens rather than keywords (loss ratio rises). Prefilling the answer template yields 0.9 keyword leakage under standard unlearning. Diversified unlearning brings leakage to 0.3 at step 25 and 0.0 after, indistinguishable from the base query.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Unlearning suppresses surface templates more than content; supplying the template prefix exposes the retained content, and syntactic diversification of the forget set removes this.

record.problems: Several relevant curves are presented only as figures, without numerical values in the text. The safety-training comparison measures recovery of synthetic factual targets, not safety refusals or harmful-request compliance.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports extensive factual-relearning curves and utility results across additional models, datasets, metrics, and unlearning settings. They were not extracted because they do not measure the safety behavior in the claim; the relevant safety-training comparison and template-injection results are retained above.

untested.parts: No fine-tuning on harmful examples and no harmful-compliance measure.
Benign fine-tuning is tested only for recovery of unlearned facts, not for harmful compliance or refusal erosion.
No per-token KL between aligned and base models on harmful prompts.
The prefill (template injection) is tested for factual keyword leakage only. No harmful-refusal bypass; no suffixes or decoding changes.
The LoRA vs full relearning comparison concerns recovery speed of facts, not localization of safety.
The template-vs-keyword suppression mechanism concerns unlearning, not the shallowness of safety alignment.
Syntactic diversification is evaluated for unlearning robustness, not for deepening safety alignment.

record.verdict_notes: There are analogies to the claim but no test of it. Template-token suppression resembles shallow, surface-level alignment (V3/V6), and template prefilling resembles a prefilling attack (V4). But the behaviour measured is factual recall after unlearning, not safety refusal of harmful requests. The WMDP experiment concerns hazardous knowledge but measures knowledge recovery by LLM-judge scores, not harmful compliance. The record's 'discusses'/T6 classification and all rows as ['none'] are correct.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not fine-tune safety-trained chat models on harmful examples or measure harmful-request compliance.
The paper fine-tunes models on benign relearning data, including models trained with IDK and DPO, but measures recovery of forgotten factual keywords rather than harmful compliance or safety refusal.
No per-token KL comparison between aligned and base models is reported.
The template-injection prompt is tested for factual leakage after unlearning, not for harmful-request refusal; suffixes and decoding changes are not tested.
LoRA relearning is compared with full-parameter relearning, but safety behavior is not localized to weights or ranks.
The paper's proposed mechanism concerns syntactic template suppression during unlearning, not why safety alignment is shallow.
Syntactic diversification is tested for robustness of factual unlearning, not for deepening safety behavior beyond initial response tokens.

rows.measure: Attack Success Rate for target keyword leakage
rows.baseline: Base query; numeric value not stated
rows.note: The text says template injection yields higher leakage than the base query. This is factual leakage after unlearning, not a compliant opening bypassing a safety refusal.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for shallow_safety_alignment. Template injection produces target-keyword leakage of 0.9, exceeding the base query; the base-query rate is not stated numerically.
source_check.problem: Factual keyword leakage after unlearning does not measure bypass of harmful-request refusal.

rows.check: The text says injection leakage 'becomes indistinguishable from the base query' (0.3 at step 25). Against its stated baseline, the injection effect is absent, not partial. 0.3 is the absolute leakage level.

source_check.correct: state=cannot_determine for shallow_safety_alignment. At step 25, absolute factual leakage is 0.3; the authors describe template injection as indistinguishable from the base query, so the incremental injection effect is absent.
source_check.problem: The baseline-relative interpretation is accurate, but this factual measure cannot determine any safety-alignment claim version.
